summary.text: Radio astronomy is a subfield of astronomy that studies celestial objects using radio waves.
It started in 1933, when Karl Jansky at Bell Telephone Laboratories reported radiation coming from the Milky Way.
It uses radio telescopes alone or linked together, and linking them gives high angular resolution because an interferometer's resolving power is set by the distance between its components.

items.prompt: Radio astronomers only receive signals from space. A team that sends out a signal and also listens for the echo is doing what?

options.label: Radar astronomy, an active kind of observation
Radio astronomy, a passive kind of observation
Interferometry, a way to link telescopes
Aperture synthesis, a way to build a dish

items.explain: Radio astronomy is passive, receiving only, while radar astronomy is active, transmitting and receiving.

items.prompt: An engineer's antenna records a hiss that peaks about every 24 hours, so he suspects the Sun. What shows the Sun is not the source?

options.label: The hiss gets noticeably louder once it is dark
The hiss only shows up during the summer months
The hiss fades whenever thunderstorms move past
It repeats every 23 hours 56 minutes, like a fixed star

items.explain: The signal did not follow the Sun's 24-hour cycle exactly, and its repeat time matched a sidereal day, the time for fixed astronomical objects to pass the antenna again.

items.prompt: A group links several small antennas spread across a wide area. What mainly decides how sharp their combined view is?

options.label: The size of each single antenna
The distance between the antennas
The brightness of the daytime sky
The color of the dishes' surfaces

items.explain: The resolving power of an interferometer is set by the distance between its components, rather than their size.

items.prompt: In 1902 physicists decided that radio waves from the Sun and other sky sources could not be picked up from the ground. What was their reasoning?

options.label: The Sun is too hot to give off radio waves
Radio waves cannot cross empty space
A reflecting layer in the sky would send them back into space
No antenna big enough could be built

items.explain: After the radio-reflecting ionosphere was found, they concluded it would bounce astronomical radio transmissions back into space, making them undetectable.

items.prompt: After finding that the Sun and other stars were not big radio emitters, what did Jansky suggest was behind the Milky Way's signal?

options.label: Interstellar gas and dust in the galaxy
A powerful radio station on Earth
Nearby thunderstorms in the atmosphere
The Moon reflecting sunlight

items.explain: He concluded the interference might come from interstellar gas and dust, through thermal agitation of charged particles.

items.prompt: During wartime, two researchers detected the Sun's radio waves, yet a backyard amateur published his findings first. Why?

options.label: His dish was much bigger
The two researchers were wrong
Journals took work only from amateurs
Wartime radar secrecy bound the two but not him

items.explain: Both researchers were bound by wartime security surrounding radar, so Reber, who was not, published first.

beats.prompt: This reasoning about radio waves from space has one wrong step. Which one?

steps.text: In 1902 physicists found a layer in the sky that reflects radio waves.
Radio waves from the Sun would have to cross that layer to reach the ground.
So the layer lets them pass straight through to antennas below.
So solar radio waves should be easy to detect from the ground.

beats.explain: The physicists concluded the opposite: the layer would bounce astronomical radio transmissions back into space, making them undetectable.

beats.idea: Radio astronomy listens passively to radio waves from space, and linking antennas sharpens the view.

paragraphs.heading: Listening to the sky
paragraphs.text: Radio astronomy studies objects in space using radio waves. It is passive, meaning it only receives, unlike radar astronomy, which both sends signals out and receives them. Its finds include stars and galaxies, plus whole new kinds of object such as radio galaxies, quasars, pulsars and masers. It also discovered the cosmic microwave background radiation, which is seen as evidence for the Big Bang theory.

paragraphs.heading: A hiss on the line
paragraphs.text: The field began by chance. Karl Jansky, newly hired as a radio engineer at Bell Telephone Laboratories, was asked to study static that might disturb short wave voice calls across the Atlantic. His large directional antenna kept recording a repeating hiss that nobody could explain. Because it peaked about every 24 hours, he first suspected the Sun.

paragraphs.heading: The clue in the timing
paragraphs.text: Closer study showed the signal repeated every 23 hours and 56 minutes, not every 24 hours. His friend, the astrophysicist Albert Melvin Skellett, noticed that this was exactly a sidereal day: the time "fixed" objects such as stars take to pass in front of the antenna again as Earth turns. By comparing with star maps, Jansky found the signal peaked when his antenna faced the densest part of the Milky Way, in Sagittarius. He announced this in April 1933, and radio astronomy was born.

paragraphs.heading: Early builders
paragraphs.text: In 1937 Grote Reber, a radio amateur inspired by Jansky, built a dish-shaped radio telescope 9 meters (30 ft) across in his backyard in Wheaton, Illinois. He first repeated Jansky's observations and then made the first survey of the sky at radio frequencies. In 1942 a British Army research officer, James Stanley Hey, became the first to detect radio waves from the Sun. Jansky is honoured in the basic unit of flux density, the jansky (Jy).

paragraphs.heading: Linking telescopes
paragraphs.text: The work relies on large antennas called radio telescopes, used alone or joined together. Joining them through methods called interferometry and aperture synthesis gives high angular resolution, or fine detail, because the resolving power depends on how far apart the parts are rather than how big each one is. Martin Ryle and Antony Hewish, of the Cavendish Astrophysics Group, developed a method called Earth-rotation aperture synthesis. The Cambridge Interferometer was used to map the radio sky, and from that map came the 2C and 3C Cambridge catalogues of radio sources.

paragraphs.heading: The heart of the galaxy
paragraphs.text: In the 1950s, Jansky's strongest source, one of the brightest in the radio sky, was named Sagittarius A. Today it is thought to come from ions orbiting a massive black hole at the center of our galaxy. That point is now called Sagittarius A*.
